Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Conversation, family & daily routines

argument noun

a quarrel

also quarrel, row, squabble, dispute, have an argument, argue, get into an argument

classical

Plin. Ep. 8.5.1: sine jūrgiō sine offēnsā
Ter. Ph. 778: dē jūrgiō silētur

1jūrgium, jūrgō: long u (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). From jūs and agō: de Vaan 317, s.v. jūs, writes jūrgium and (ob)jūrgāre, which “seem to be based on a noun” meaning “bringing the oath”.

jūrgium1, jūrgiī n.

noun, second declension

a quarrel, a row

A quarrel between people who otherwise wish each other well, at home or between neighbours: Cicero sets jūrgium against līs, a dispute between enemies or at law (Rep. 4.8, quoted by Nonius; Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • jūrgō1, jūrgāre, jūrgāvī, jūrgātum — quarrel, have a row

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. And. 389: Cedo quid jūrgābit tēcum?

  • altercor, altercārī, altercātus sum — argue, have words (with someone)

    verb, first conjugation, deponent; cum and the ablative, or inter sē · also used · classical · Publil. Sent. N 58, quoted by Gell. 17.14.4: nimium altercandō; Traupman 273: altercātiō, argument

    The noun altercātiō is a sharp exchange of words (see debate).

  • in lītem ambiguam dēscendere — get into an argument

    also used · modern · Traupman 93

    Traupman’s phrase; not found in Lewis & Short or the loci. Līs is a dispute, especially at law; dēscendere in, to come down into (a contest).

  • altercātiō, altercātiōnis f. — a dispute, a war of words

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 273

    Lewis & Short notes that Cicero uses it in his letters and philosophy, but in his speeches prefers disceptātiō and contentiō.

  • rixa, rixae f. — a squabble, a brawl

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Traupman 384; Cic. Fam. 9.22.1: Acadēmīae nostrae cum Zēnōne magna rixa est (Lewis & Short); Traupman 367

  • rixor, rixārī, rixātus sum — squabble, brawl, wrangle

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Lucr. 6.1286: rixantēs (Lewis & Short); Traupman 384; Cic. de Or. 2.240: cum esset cum eō dē amiculā rixātus (Lewis & Short); Traupman 367

Examples

  • vīxit cum hāc trīgintā novem annīs sine jūrgiō sine offēnsā

    he lived with her for thirty-nine years without a quarrel or a hurtPlin. Ep. 8.5.1

  • nimium altercandō vēritās āmittitur

    in too much arguing the truth gets lostPublil. Sent. N 58, quoted by Gell. 17.14.4

See also argument, stop squabbling!, debate.

SourcesQuotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-publilius, loci-gellius), as checked there against the editions they name.

Publilius is cited as the loci collection numbers him, by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library text; from N onwards that numbering differs from Meyer’s.

Plin. Ep. 8.5.1, Ter. And. 389 and Ph. 778 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 93, 273.

Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 317.
